source: Zhou et al. (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (re-read for gaps 1, 2, 6)
finding: The paper uses greedy decoding at temperature 0 on open-weight models only. Its early-stopping test (Section 5.4) uses the same AIME data that defined the trace indicators. No held-out split, no second seed, no paired test on accuracy.
numbers: Claims indicator-based early stopping reaches 97% of peak accuracy with 60% of compute (Figure 7, AIME). The limitations section says only open-weight models were tested and that causal mechanisms need controlled interventions.
limits: The paper itself did not run the checks in gaps 1 and 6. The 97% at 60% result is in-sample.
agent_relevance: A stop rule built from Zhou's indicators is untested. Treat the 12K peak and the indicator thresholds as hypotheses to measure on our own agent.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (re-read full text)
finding: Open-budget runs were repeated over 3 random seeds with 95% CIs. Claude Sonnet 4 'willing to be turned off' fell 60% to 47% as reasoning grew. o3 rose 72% to 76%. DeepSeek R1 stayed at 71-72%. The safety shift is model-specific, not shared; the paper text says the accuracy pattern holds across all nine models on constructed tasks.
numbers: Budgets 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384 tokens; 3 seeds per budget; Misleading Python used 500 questions across 3 seeds (1500 samples). Sonnet 4 qualitative analysis compared no reasoning with a 16,384 budget.
quote: limitations concerning the naturalness of the experiments
limits: Same group as the original, so not an outside replication. Tasks are synthetic by the authors' own admission. Divergence between Sonnet 4, o3 and R1 inside the one paper shows the safety effect does not transfer across models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 half answered: same-paper replication over seeds and five budgets yes, across models no (o3 and R1 do not show it), outside the lab not found. Gap 1 partly answered for constructed tasks: three seeds, CIs reported.

source: Srivastava et al. (2026 v3) Do LLMs Overthink Basic Math Reasoning? LLMThinkBench
finding: On 14 basic-math tasks with dynamically generated items, raising the reasoning-effort setting of closed frontier models gives a plateau, not a decline. 53 models tested; reasoning models use about 18x more tokens than non-reasoning ones while sometimes scoring lower.
numbers: GPT-5: 97% at medium and 97% at high effort. o3: 97% at low, medium and high, with 8% more tokens at high. Gemini-2.5-Flash: 92% (off) to 93% to 92% (max). Gemini-2.5-Pro peaks at its lowest tested budget (128 tokens, 90%).
limits: Basic arithmetic only; effort levels are coarse, so they cannot see a 12K to 16K drop. Not a test of Zhou's flip ratio.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, other models: GPT-5, o3, o3-mini, o4-mini and Gemini 2.5 show no gain and no loss. On easy tasks overthinking looks like waste, not damage. This weakens a universal accuracy-loss claim.

source: Qwen Team (2025) Qwen3 Technical Report, section 4.7 thinking budget
finding: Qwen3-235B-A22B shows 'scalable and smooth' gains as the thinking budget rises on four benchmarks in maths, coding and STEM, up to 32K tokens. The authors expect gains beyond 32K. Budget stop inserts a fixed stop-thinking sentence and the model answers from its partial reasoning.
numbers: Figure 2, budgets up to 32K tokens, one model (235B MoE). No per-problem flips and no CIs in the text.
limits: Vendor report, curves not tables in the text; single model; no flip analysis, so a small drop could hide inside smooth curves. Uses the model's own trained budget control, unlike Zhou's forced Wait.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, Qwen3: no sign of decline to 32K on the vendor's own plots. Either the effect is model-specific (R1-32B, s1-32B) or too small to see on curves. The 'peak near 12K' is not a general number.

source: Jurayj, Cheng, Van Durme (2025) Is That Your Final Answer? Test-Time Scaling Improves Selective Question Answering
finding: R1-32B and S1-32B on AIME 2024+2025 (60 problems), temperature 0, budgets 500 to 8000 tokens in steps of 100. With threshold 0 (always answer) accuracy rises steadily with budget. At high confidence thresholds, accuracy of answered items can fall as budget grows, but that is because more hard questions get answered. Confidence in correct answers rises with budget for R1-32B; S1-32B separates correct from incorrect less well.
numbers: Thresholds 0, 0.5, 0.95; budgets 500-8000; GPQA in appendix; greedy decoding.
limits: Range stops at 8K, below Zhou's 12K peak, so it cannot see the decline. Same two models and greedy decoding as Zhou. Opened in full this session (earlier only a snippet).
agent_relevance: A confidence-gated answer is a usable stop signal for R1-32B but weaker for s1-32B. Gap 6 hint: signal quality is model-dependent.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: With repeated Wait-style extension, accuracy first rises then falls on GSM-8K, MATH-500 and AIME 2024 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, -7B and Llama-8B. Authors explain it with output variance: entropy of the answer distribution rises (MATH-500 entropy 0.02 to 0.12 in the early rise), so the early gain is partly a variance effect. At equal budget, parallel thinking with a vote is better.
numbers: Parallel thinking: GSM8K, R1-Distill-1.5B, same budget of 385 standard tokens, +10.1 points while extended thinking falls. Abstract says up to 20% higher accuracy, intro says up to 22% at a 16K budget.
limits: Small distilled models only, stylised probabilistic model, not causal proof. Seeds not stated in the text I searched.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partial: an equal-token one-chain vs k-chains test, but only for small distilled models and without NoThinking-first or short-m@k arms.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi, Schwartz (2025) Don't Overthink it. Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Four models (LN-Super-49B, R1-32B, QwQ-32B, R1-670B) on AIME24, AIME25, HMMT and GPQA-D. Equal thinking-compute comparison of short-1@k, short-3@k and majority@k. short-1@k beats majority at low compute and loses at high compute in 3 of 4 models. short-3@k beats majority at lower compute across all models and budgets. The sequential (non-batched) setting keeps the ordering.
numbers: LN-Super-49B: short-1@k 57% accuracy with about 60% of the compute majority@k needs. short-1@k beats majority up to 45k, 60k and 100k total thinking tokens on R1-32B, QwQ-32B, R1-670B. QwQ-32B at 80k tokens: short-3@k +2% over majority. R1-670B at 100k: about +4%. LN-Super-49B k=5: short-1@k about 50% less time, +1.5%. R1-32B k=5: short-3@k 33% faster. GPQA-D shortest vs longest chain of the same question: 69.1 vs 57.6 (LN-Super-49B).
quote: within a single question (both easy and hard), shorter thinking is preferable
limits: No NoThinking arm and no single long chain at equal tokens. Shorter chains may be shorter because the model was confident (selection). Seeds not reported in the lines I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 half closed: short-m@k vs majority vote is measured at equal compute on four models. The remaining arms (one long chain, NoThinking-first) are not in the same table.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Table 2: thinking length by difficulty tercile and correctness
finding: Questions were split into three equal groups by the model's own success rate. Inside each tercile and inside each question, correct answers are shorter than incorrect ones. Across terciles, harder questions use up to 2.9x more tokens. This is the nearest thing to a matched-difficulty test.
numbers: Thousands of tokens, correct/incorrect/all. LN-Super-49B: easy 5.3/11.1/5.7, medium 11.4/17.1/14.6, hard 12.4/16.8/16.6. R1-32B: easy 8.4 (correct only), medium 14.8/21.6, hard 19.1/22.8. QwQ-32B hard 23.0/31.7.
limits: Still correlational: a chain can be long because it is going wrong, not wrong because it is long. Difficulty is measured by the model's own success rate.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly answered: with difficulty held fixed by question, length still separates wrong from right. That favours 'length is a symptom' over 'length is a cause'; it cannot show that cutting length helps. Zhou's forced extension tests cause; Hassid controls difficulty. Neither does both.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking
finding: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, skipping the thinking block (NoThinking) beats Thinking at pass@1 when tokens are matched and small, and beats it at pass@k for all budgets with k>1. At about 3,500 tokens Thinking wins at pass@1. LiveCodeBench is an exception: Thinking wins even at low budget because disabling the box does not cut tokens much.
numbers: AMC23 at 700 tokens: 51.3 vs 28.9 pass@1. Matched budgets: AIME25 1800 and 3500, AMC23 700 and 1700, OlympiadBench 800 and 1900, LCB 800 and 3400. NoThinking plus parallel scaling matched Thinking-without-budget with 7x lower latency (perfect verifier) and 4x fewer tokens on MiniF2F and ProofNet.
limits: One model family (R1-Distill-Qwen-32B). Low-end budget forcing may favour NoThinking. Perfect-verifier results are an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partial: the NoThinking-first arm is measured at matched tokens with parallel scaling. It wins when tokens are short. It is not in the same table as short-m@k or one long chain beyond 3.5K.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models: Do they Truly Possess Test-Time Scaling Capabilities?
finding: For QwQ, R1-Distill (32B, 14B, 1.5B) and LIMO, correct solutions are often shorter than incorrect ones for the same question. Forcing extra rounds of revision: accuracy of QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5B keeps falling; 32B, 14B and LIMO rise early then oscillate. Successful revision (wrong to right) stays under 10%. For QwQ and R1-1.5B the failed-revision rate (right to wrong) is higher than the successful rate. When the first answer is wrong, R1-32B and R1-14B keep it in over 70% of cases.
numbers: Share of revisions that stick to the original wrong answer: R1-32B 72%, R1-14B 70%, R1-1.5B 58%, QwQ 32%, LIMO 54%. Forced continuation of 40 steps on AIME. Parallel scaling gives better coverage than sequential. Shortest Majority Vote beats plain majority vote on AIME and GPQA at 2 and 16 samples (Table 2).
quote: correct solutions are often shorter than incorrect ones for the same questions
limits: Early-2025 models; revision is induced by prompting 'Wait' or 'Alternatively', not natural. The benefit in 32B and 14B comes mainly from revising short solutions.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 (indirect): the cost side of revising is measured. A gate that blocks revision would remove failed revisions (right to wrong) but also the under-10% successful ones. For strong models net revision benefit is positive early, so a gate should block late revisions, not all.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: A training-free stop rule: at reasoning-transition points the model writes a trial answer, and generation stops if the mean token probability of that answer exceeds 0.95. One threshold for all 10 benchmarks and 11 models. Reduces CoT length 19.1% to 80.1% and changes accuracy by +0.3 to +5.0 against full generation (vanilla, 16,384 cap).
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B overall 69.2 at 61.5% of tokens vs vanilla 64.2 at 100% and TCC 67.1 at 83.0%. Qwen3-14B: DEER 83.7 at 57.1% vs vanilla 82.8; TCC 83.3 at 93.1%. QwQ-32B: DEER 84.0 at 80.9% vs vanilla 82.6; TCC 80.4 at 99.7%. AMC23, AIME24, AIME25 use 4 sampling rounds.
limits: Math, GPQA-D and LCB only. The 'fixed budget' baseline (TCC) is a prompt, not hard truncation, and models ignore it on AIME. Threshold was set once, not tuned per set. 4 rounds is small for 30 problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 2, half closed in math: an answer-confidence stop rule beat the full-length run at lower mean tokens on three models and beat a token-prompt baseline. But see d12: it failed outside math.

source: Shen and Yao (2026) Not All Test-Time Compute Is Evidence (DIA), Table 2 baselines
finding: An independent comparison on 7 benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B found that DEER and Dynasor (answer-stability stop) did not raise average accuracy against full CoT. DEER lost most on knowledge and multi-hop tasks. Dynasor used more tokens on average.
numbers: Qwen3-4B average accuracy: CoT 70.77 at 1.00 tokens; DEER 67.76 at 0.87; Dynasor 69.33 at 1.52. Qwen3-8B: CoT 72.50; DEER 70.64 at 0.82; Dynasor 70.46 at 1.26. MMLU-Pro Qwen3-4B: CoT 68.00, DEER 63.14. MuSiQue Qwen3-4B: CoT 59.00, DEER 51.67. GPQA-D Qwen3-4B: DEER 56.06 vs CoT 51.01 at 1.60x tokens. Each dataset 100-300 questions.
limits: Authors' own method competes (DIA), so baselines may be weaker. Small Qwen3 models. Single run per cell; no CIs in Table 2.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 negative: outside competition maths, existing stop rules cost accuracy at equal or lower tokens. A stop rule that wins on AIME may not win on our mixed tasks. Test per domain.

source: Shen and Yao (2026) DIA Section 2.2-2.3 and Table 1: self-selection and initial-answer persistence
finding: When Qwen3-8B had to choose between its own intermediate answer and its final answer, it chose the final one in over 95% of disagreements, even when the earlier answer was correct, with near-100% confidence on wrong choices. Heterogeneous reviewers comparing full traces also chose the final-stage answer in over 90% of disagreements. Independent re-solving by a panel of other models worked.
numbers: Table 1: MuSR final-stage preference 97.7%, self-select accuracy 44.1%, right when earlier correct and final wrong 0.0%, right when final correct 93.8%. MMLU-Pro 95.1%, 63.4%, 6.7%, 96.2%. Wrong-choice confidence 100% in both. Initially wrong answer retained after CoT (Qwen3-8B): MMLU-Pro 26.23%, MuSR 61.90%. DIA activated on 17% of items; beat CoT in 12 of 14 settings; average 73.82 vs 70.77 (4B), 74.95 vs 72.50 (8B), at 2.62-2.68x tokens.
quote: More compute from the same model is therefore not more evidence
limits: The intermediate answer is extracted by a confidence criterion, not by natural oscillation. Two small Qwen3 models. Author-proposed method.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a 'verify before revising' gate built as the same model judging its two answers will not work, since it nearly always prefers the later answer. A working gate needs independent re-solving or an external check, which costs about 2.6x tokens here.

source: Oh and Lee (2026) Adaptive Stopping of Streamed Reasoning for Language Model Agents (StreamStop)
finding: In closed-loop agent tasks (WebShop, ScienceWorld) a learned stop head reading the reasoning prefix achieved higher success than validation-selected fixed budgets, and about the same as full thinking at 42% fewer reasoning tokens on WebShop with Qwen3.8-27B. On WebShop with Nemotron it beat full thinking in success with fewer tokens, which the authors link to overthinking.
numbers: WebShop Qwen3.8-27B: Full 43.0 +/-2.2 at 5945 tok/ep; StreamStop(0.99) 42.8 +/-0.8 at 3464; Const-M 35.0 at 1519; Dynasor-CoT variants 31.7 to 39.0 at 1444-3348. Nemotron-3-Nano: Full 34.5 at 5374; StreamStop 37.0 +/-4.6 at 3727. ScienceWorld Qwen3.8: Full 52.1 at 45380; StreamStop 49.2-50.8 at 20757-23680. Mean and SD over evaluation seeds; test split separate from validation used to choose baselines.
limits: Gains are within one seed SD in several cells. Tokens are not equal across arms: fixed budgets are cheaper. Absolute success is low (35-52%). Model names as given in the paper.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 7: the first held-out agent test where a learned stop rule beats fixed budgets and ties full thinking. Also the first agent evidence that less thinking can score higher than full (Nemotron). Needs a trained head, so not a pure scaffold rule.

source: Wen et al. (2026) MetaCtrl: LLMs Can Reason Better and More Concisely with a Metacognitive Controller
finding: A small RL-trained controller decides continue, simplify, skip or conclude on a frozen reasoner. It raised accuracy and cut generated tokens on seven benchmarks and transferred without retraining to unseen reasoners.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (seen): +4.7 average points, -53.3% length. Unseen Qwen3-14B: +2.9 points, -50.3%. Qwen3-8B 67.0 to 70.5 and Qwen3-14B 71.0 to 74.1, tokens -50.0% and -53.7%, versus ASAG -31.2% and -26.9%. Unseen R1-Distill-Qwen-32B: 62.1 vs vanilla 62.3, length -45.6%.
limits: Needs RL training of the controller. Benchmarks are small (AIME24 has 30 problems). Seeds and CIs not in the text I read. Some baseline numbers are copied from earlier papers.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a controller with stop and continue actions beats the unforced run at about half the tokens and transfers to unseen models. Still not a pure rule, and not a same-mean-token comparison against a fixed budget.

source: Bulut (2026) It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories
finding: A pre-registered, restart-controlled study of two small open models on 89 MATH problems. 'Breakthrough' moments in traces are mostly budget artifacts. Early-window internal signals carry no outcome information beyond problem difficulty. A trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873 on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations, inside the published probe range; a matched reconstruction of a published positive falls to chance within a problem.
numbers: 178 problem-model cells, 1 of 178 prefix-limited. Continuing own prefix beats restart at matched budget 9 of 9 (compute compression). Pooled AUROC 0.849 vs within-problem 0.496 at t=4. Models: Gemma-4 E4B and Ministral-3 3B, 4-bit, 16K-token traces.
quote: High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information
limits: Small models, MATH only, early-window probes rather than oscillation counters. Does not test Zhou's flip ratio directly; cites Zhou as related work.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 6: strong warning that any trace indicator must be tested within problem, not pooled. Zhou's r=0.78 was pooled on the defining sample, the pattern this paper shows can be difficulty in disguise. Judge any oscillation stop rule by within-problem gain.

source: Gonzalez i Catala et al. (2026) Answer-Distribution Trajectories: A Stochastic-Dynamics View of LLM Reasoning
finding: Sixteen open models on GSM8K, ARC, SVAMP and MATH: the model-task pairs with highest accuracy switch their dominant answer less, move less and commit earlier; the shortest-CoT pairs switch more and commit later. Variance in switching is largest within a model-task pair, not between models.
numbers: Standardised means: high accuracy Nswitch -0.68 SD, commitment time -0.53 SD, accuracy 78.8%, CoT length 240; short-CoT pairs Nswitch +1.03 SD, accuracy 18.6%, length 56. Instruction tuning gives the clearest shift to fewer switches; higher temperature delays commitment.
limits: Small models, short chains, easy benchmarks; answers estimated by Monte Carlo rollouts; correlational. Workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 8: across 16 models, answer switching goes with lower accuracy, which supports an oscillation monitor as a cross-model signal. It is not a flip-ratio replication and says nothing about long traces.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: In parallel sampling, token-confidence filtering and early termination of low-confidence traces cuts tokens against full majority voting while keeping or raising accuracy. Evaluated on Qwen3 and GPT-OSS models.
numbers: AIME 2025 with GPT-OSS-120B: DeepConf@512 99.9% vs cons@512 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8% (offline mode). Online mode reduces generated tokens by up to 84.7% with equal or better accuracy. The paper notes models can be confident on wrong paths.
limits: 512 traces is a high-compute regime; best numbers are the favourable cases. Not a single-chain stop rule.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 5 partial: a stop rule inside the k-chains design (kill weak chains early) beats plain vote at fewer tokens. It joins the parallel and early-exit ideas.

source: Citation scan of Zhou et al. 2604.10739 via the Semantic Scholar graph API (gap 10)
finding: 21 citing papers were listed, all from 2026. I opened the five closest (2609.03436, 2610.23213, 2610.27981, 2609.37304, 2610.19872). Each cites Zhou as motivation or related work. None re-runs the flip ratio or the 67.5% audit, and none reports a failed replication.
numbers: 21 citing papers, 2026-04 to 2026-10. StreamStop and DIA cite Zhou for abandoning a correct answer. MetaCtrl cites it among works showing deviation from a correct solution. Bulut cites it for non-monotone thinking-length effects.
limits: One API snapshot, may be incomplete. I did not open all 21. Absence of a replication among these titles is not proof none exists.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: no replication and no failed replication found. Zhou's flip-ratio result is cited but not reproduced as of November 2026.

source: Guo, Wu, Yiu (2026) The Deterministic Horizon: When Extended Reasoning Fails and Tool Delegation Becomes Necessary
finding: On deterministic state-tracking tasks, longer chain-of-thought hurts past a depth, and delegating steps to tools works far better. Abstract page only was read.
numbers: Twelve models, eight task domains. Tool-integrated reasoning 76-94% on PermutationProbe vs 17-42% for neural CoT. Deterministic horizon d* between 19 and 31 at alpha 0.5. Fine-tuning on optimal-length traces helps under 3 points.
limits: Opened the arXiv abstract page only, not the full text. Synthetic permutation tasks, not judgment or planning.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 (non-math): a non-math domain where extra reasoning steps fail by depth. For our agent: hand deterministic bookkeeping to a tool instead of thinking longer.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs (re-read for gap 8)
finding: Wrong answers show far more thought switching. The thought-switching-penalty decoder (TIP) lifts accuracy without extra training. The paper varies penalty strength and duration but does not sweep the total token budget, so overthinking and underthinking are not traded off in one curve.
numbers: o1-like models use 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches in incorrect answers. QwQ-32B-Preview AIME24: 38.3 to 44.1 with TIP at the chosen setting (strength 3, duration 600). Too long a penalty at high strength lowers accuracy (strength 20, duration above 300).
limits: One method, a few models, no budget sweep. The penalty itself can be too strong.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: no paper I found runs a budget sweep with a switch penalty and a stop rule together. The ADT paper (d17) gives cross-model support that fewer switches go with higher accuracy.

source: Zhang and Zhang (2026) RCCM: Diagnosing Gains and Harms in Reasoning-Prompt Transfer
finding: Aggregate accuracy hides question-level rescues and harms. The same prompt strategy can rescue a few errors on one model and harm many correct answers on another. The paper reports paired rescue/harm counts, the accounting that a verify-before-revise gate needs.
numbers: Qwen: a strategy rescues five and harms 37. Phi: CoD rescues 20 CoT errors and harms five. Llama: CoD rescues 15 and harms 24. 120 development questions per deployment, five deployments, nine strategies, MATH500; 60 further questions for follow-ups.
limits: Small samples, small models, prompt strategies not extended reasoning. A reporting method, not a gate test.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 method: log rescues and harms per question for any gate we test; report net flips, not accuracy only.

source: Mia and Amini (2026) Don't Overthink, Don't Underthink: Toward Adaptive Reasoning in Agentic AI
finding: In a LangGraph agent on MATH-500 and GAIA with small models, cases labelled over-reasoning cost more tokens without extra accuracy, and under-reasoning cases go with wrong or incomplete answers. Labels come from the authors' rubric.
numbers: MATH-500: Phi-4-reasoning over-reasoning rate 89.40%, 2220 reasoning tokens, hit the token limit in 482 of 500 (96.40%) with 92.12% accuracy on limit-hit cases; Qwen3.5-4B 68.00%. GAIA accuracy at most about 12-13%.
limits: Descriptive, no matched controls, no budget sweep, GAIA scores near floor. Weak evidence; included only because it is agentic.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the pattern is claimed in agents but not measured with controls. Do not count as evidence of harm.
